doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
title: 1939 Exposition: Benny Goodman and Buddy Rich
summary: Basie and Goodman play Treasure Island; he reflects on Buddy Rich's instinct and vaudeville background.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: perform at our Exposition. They were at Exposition 1939 World Exposition at Treasure Island. And I was blessed because I was in it all night. I got to go there and see that. Benny Goodman came up, by then Krupa and Harry James had left him but he had Nick Fatool on drums and Fletcher Henderson was playing piano. And that was a kind of memorable because our show was at the Golden Gate Theater. And Goodman was at Treasure Island. So that meant you taxied between the two. And I don’t know how we did it because we didn’t have any money. In 1939 who had any money? But we would go see Goodman and then we’d go to the theater, because you know Buddy Rich was with him at the time. And even then, on records, Buddy Rich really impressed me on records because of his fire and his solos. I didn’t realize at that time there was more to him than appeared. He played for the band. He knew just exactly what to play, I don’t care what the song was, I don’t care what the style was, he had an instinct. But of course part of it too was exposure. Because he grew up in Vaudeville. And he used to watch, from what they say, he learned from watching all of the Vaudeville drummers throughout the country. And these guys, you know, they had all kinds of sound effects, because before the talkies you know they had—
Juggling and all that kind of stuff.

Oh yeah. Making the thunder noise when on the screen there was a thunder. And the rain noises. And then of course when you had everything, your juggling acts and your dog acts and they had to do everything, with the whistle — whoop and the rolls, that sounded like paper tearing, you know, really fine, symphony style rolls. But so Rich, and in later years I realized that he was just more than a noisemaker. This guy was — he knew exactly what the band needed or what the musical occasion called for to play, and the act, he could play any act. Because he was a tap dancer himself. And he had seen all the acts. He had grown up with all the different routines. But anyhow so back and forth we were, back and forth. So that was the — and with Basie’s, then the guys stayed here. So although I didn’t get to know them, friends of mine, they really got to know the fellas in the Basie band. And I was underage too so I couldn’t go in the night clubs. Couldn’t hang out in the bars, or the watering holes.
